I'm not his counsel and I have no right to interfere but I thought it only fair of me to raise that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reassure you, I was not about to ask him a question that had to do with the specific events that happy in Srebrenica. So I think he can be called back in. Safely but called back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps my reaction was premature in that case, but I believed at the time it was warranted given his position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam usher, you can call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I would like -- Mr. Registrar can switch it on. We are going to talk about your position vis-a-vis the Tribunal. Do you want us to go into private session or do you want us to talk publicly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, at the beginning of the trial before you came into court, the Chamber was advised that you are a suspect before the Tribunal. And that therefore before the question was put to you, Mr. Lukic was concerned that you be warned about your rights against self-incrimination. And that being the case, that there are certain rights that you are entitled to, you can either insist on having a lawyer advise you on whether to answer a question that's put to you if you feel uncomfortable about it, or you may waive the right to have a lawyer and decide for yourself whether it's a question you want to answer or not want to answer. So I'm saying to you, the Judge is going to put the question to you, you decide whether it's a question that you would like to answer. I know you've told us that you have answered this question in two statements that you have made to the OTP already, but the question was not complete just yet, so listen to the question and take your time to think about your rights. Thank you so much. Thank you, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skrbic, I do not intend to ask you anything about a possible participation in the events in Srebrenica. I'm more interested in the information that was done later on after that in Republika Srpska as to the events. I readily imagine that what had happened was soon known within the army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daily information, Your Honour, was contained in daily combat reports. Those daily combat reports were not available to me for inspection because they never reached my sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, the fact that the events had occurred and the information that may have been conveyed within the army about that, may it have been impact on the morale of the troops on recruiting on possible requests to leave the VRS? Did soldiers not try to leave then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to judge that, the specific topic that you have addressed. Not all of the soldiers knew what had happened. Not in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did not see or perceive that there was an increase in requests to leave the VRS then? Or just after that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now a total different question. Are you a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to be. It was called citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was the exact title of my nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean to say is that you were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were you a volunteer? Did you volunteer to serve in the army of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war started, Your Honour, I received an order that I told you about. The order was not carried out because my own chief General Vuk Obradovic stepped in to see that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that. I understood that you were ordered to leave and that eventually only left one year later. But my question was whether you immediately volunteered to go? We were told indeed that many JNA military and VJ military volunteered to go without having received the order to go first?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I merely expressed my desire to my chief, General Vuk Obradovic. He then told me that at the time I should not be considering that. The next time I went of my own accord, Your Honour. On the 17th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Skrbic. This is a question that Mr. Lukic had promised to attend to on the 16th of June and he never did. You gave testimony on that day, and unfortunately I'm not able to give you a page reference, to the effect that the Main Staff of the VRS changed to General Staff of the VRS at some stage. I would like to know when that took place.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, late in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. Long after the war was over?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I have no further questions. Mr. Lukic -- I beg your pardon. Yes, Mr. Lukic, any re-examination -- examination arising from the questions by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just to specify one thing, the answer given by the witness at page 51 to Judge Picard when she asked him about the period of Srebrenica. Further cross-examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then after that when the soldiers were trying to leave the arrest, line 19, the witness said he didn't know that that was the case, at least as far as I can tell. He said in those days and then my question, all of us here know that this was mid-July 1995. What about the following period leading up to the end of war, were there any en masse departures by officers, NCOs, or soldiers from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were departures but not on a massive scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The English suggests that this wasn't on a massive scale. When you say not a lot, I understand why the interpreters did what they did, but can you [indiscernible] this for us in relative terms. We know the figures above the rest of the war and what about from this point on, what was the comparison between earlier and later?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the VRS was about 200.000 strong at the time, but who exactly do you mean? Active duty servicemen, contractual servicemen, civilians working for the army, forgive me for I am unable to understand. It was a little bit in each of these categories, nevertheless, in my answer I was quite specific, not that many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, did you say 200.000 or 300.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 200.000, Your Honour, about 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, thank you very much, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Skrbic, finally we've got to the end of your testimony. Thank you so much for taking all the time to come and testify in the Tribunal. You've been here for a very long time and I'm sure you must be yearning to go back home taking time from your very busy schedule, and for that the Tribunal appreciates your contribution. You are now excused, you may stand down and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call our next witness who will be led by Mr. Guy-Smith. With your approval, I would like to leave the courtroom to say -- to bid farewell to Mr. Skrbic. Before his testimony he told us that he had just become a grandfather and that's why he is eager to go back home as soon as possible. I would like to congratulate him and bid him farewell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you can give him our congratulations too. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Our next witness will be Dragan Vuksic - last name V-u-k-s-i-c; first name Dragan, D-r-a-g-a-n, who I believe the usher is going to collect at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration. Madam usher, could you ask the witness to please stand up and make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The witness may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I hand you over to Mr. Guy-Smith, counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you a series of questions. If during the time that I ask you any questions you have any difficulty with the question because I've asked it poorly or for any other reason you have some misunderstanding, please stop me because I want to make sure that you are clear about what I'm asking and the Chamber is clear about what your answers are, if you are agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am agreeable to that, and thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to ask for any clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My pleasure, sir. Before we start, I understand that you also were conversant in the English language?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't like to brag, I'd rather say that in the past in order to perform some tasks, I could use English. However, time went by, I'm not getting any younger, and I would say that what I used to be able to do and what I used to know in the past has in the meantime been reduced somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. The reason I'm raising the issue with you, sir, is since I'm speaking English and you also have the benefit of somebody who is speaking B/C/S, I want to make sure that there's no confusion and would ask that you wait until you get the translation of my questions and the questions of anybody else so that you are clear about the matters that are being put to you. And if we could agree to that, that would be of some help as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am agreeable to the procedure. I'm sure that it is much better and safer for me, although, I must admit that there is a danger for me to slip into English inadvertently, and I apologise in advance if that happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I promise you that I won't be slipping into Serbian because I don't know enough and wish that I did. Can you please tell us when you were born, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we perhaps just for the record that the witness himself places his name on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely, could you place your name on the record as Judge Moloto has suggested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Dragan Vuksic. I was born on the 31st of October, 1945 in a village called Vuksici which used to be the municipality of Radatovici and that was then and it is still now in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you were born in the village of Vuksici in the municipality of Radatovici, what country was the Republic of Croatia in, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: At that time, Croatia was part of the so-called People's Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm not sure that that was the state's exact title at the time. I believe that it was the official name of Yugoslavia immediately after the war and for some time after the war, for a number of years after the war. Actually, I am not sure that it's a full title already comprised of the word federative as it would be later known.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at present, and by that I mean today, is the village in which you were born in that same country that it was at the time when you were born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, Vuksici and Radatovici and the entire area known as Zumberak was an area that was at the time and still is part of Croatia which was one of the six republics of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't hear my question or perhaps I phrased it badly. Today --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yesterday, yesterday, it is in the Republic of Croatia. Vuksici and Radatovici are both in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Vuksic. My question is, is it in the same country, not republic but country.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Now I understand your question, you are interested in the state. And if I may add to my answer and say that the place where I was born is no longer part of the state where I was born, it is now part of the state known as the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I apologise for not using the word state and using the word country instead. Could you tell us, if you know, when the place that you were born no longer became part of the state, and by that I mean the date, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I really would not be able to give you a precise answer to your question. I believe that nobody would be in a position to answer your question precisely. What I'm saying is this: The process of the dissolution of the state which was known as the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was long, it was a lengthy process, and it would be very difficult to say when the crisis started, when the state started to break up. And it is all equally difficult to say when the crisis ended or rather, when the process to break up Yugoslavia was over and that I have my own opinion on all that, and I'm sure that everybody else whose state Yugoslavia was also have their own opinions. However, there are some relevant dates which mean something to everybody. For example, the Republic of Croatia was recognised as an independent state on the 23rd of December, 1991, by the Federal Republic of Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute. And actually, before we go any further, let me warn you as well as myself, if you could keep your answers a bit crisper, I think that we both will be in better shape. If not, I think what will happen is that we may actually either lose our listeners or annoy them, neither of which I would like to do. So if you could focus with me on the questions that I ask and the answers given, I would appreciate it. Just as a little thought. All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I have not been succinct and precise. However, the question that you put to me is very important, and I really can't tell you when the area where I was born stopped being a part of the former state. I can't give you a date. I can't even give you a month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you are not able to answer a question, just say I don't know, or I'm not able to answer that question and stop there. Okay. That's what the lawyer is asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure how long we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's the time. Whether it's convenient for you, it's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to move away from the question that I asked you concerning the establishment of Croatia as a state for the moment. We will return to that at a later point in time, but I'd like to get somewhere down the road, if we could, and I'd like to discuss with you your education, and specifically in that regard your military career. So, could you tell us when you first became involved with the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I started serving in the military as an officer on the 27th of September, 1967. After having completed military academy of the land army. Before that, I was a cadet, which also implies that I was a soldier in the general sense of that term from the 20th September, 1994, until the 27th September, 1997, as I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I notice the day that you've put in here is 1994, is that correct? As a cadet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'd like to correct myself, I misspoke. The year is 1964. And I graduated from the academy in 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. And after you started your service as a military officer on the 27th of September, 1967, what I'd like to do is I'd like to go through briefly with you, if we could, the post that you held up until your ultimate retirement, which I believe you are retired. I'm assuming a fact that's presently not in evidence, so let me take care of that first. Are you presently serving in the military, Mr. Vuksic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: No, I've been retired since 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. So if we could starting in 1967, if we could briefly obtain a survey of the duties that you held and the posts that you held from 1967 up until your retirement in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it until 1997 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are correct, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first posting was as a platoon commander. I served in Delnice, a town in Croatia. I remained there only a few months, and then I was transferred to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Guy-Smith please turn his microphone off, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in Karlovac I was an acting company commander for a year. Then I was transferred to Sarajevo. I was a platoon commander in the reserve officer school for three years until 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there just for a moment. The positions that you held during this period of time were in what army, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Of course, all that was in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: And in 1971, I received an order to report to the 2nd Administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. To clarify, that was the intelligence administration. However, at the time I didn't know that the 2nd Administration was the intelligence administration, or rather that the intelligence administration was the 2nd ranking administration in the General Staff. And that was not a big mistake on my part. And then as an officer affiliated with the 2nd Administration, I was part of the military mission in Austria from 1973 to 1976. After that for a year I served as a commander of reconnaissance company unit in Belgrade, and that was the 1st Guards Division, if that means anything to anybody. And after that I served in the department for liaison with foreign military representatives from 1977 up until 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Once again, if you could, sir, could you tell us what army you were serving in during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: It was still the Yugoslav People's Army, understandably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: In 1984, I wanted to complete my education and I asked to be transferred to the armed forces centre for strategic studies and research. At the time it was a scientific institution. I started studying war doctrine. It was a post-graduate study of war doctrine. As a member of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute, if I could, please. When you said that you wanted to complete your education, what education were you in the process of attempting to complete at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I wanted to complete my military education. However, I wanted that to be done from the military and political perspective, and if that is of any importance, at the time I already started being mystified about some phenomena in the society developments concerning the position of the military in the state, the relationship between the military and the politics, and I thought that if I just continued with my routine, with my job, I would not be able to grasp the situation and to understand it better. And I think that I was absolutely right in thinking that because already in 1986, from the then position at the centre, whose name I mentioned earlier on, I became a member of the delegation of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir. You indicated that you were transferred to the armed forces centre for strategic studies in research in 1984, and at that time it was a scientific institution. When I think of science, I think of chemistry and biology, I think of hard sciences, and if you could clarify for us what you mean here by the term, "a scientific institution," I would be most appreciative.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: It was an institution for education and continuous education. It was an institution that provided education to civilians who occupied certain positions who were earmarked to perform important jobs in crisis situations or in war time. They would come for six-month educational stints in that centre. Within that centre, there was also a unit where I worked, and that was the institute for strategic research where the military and political reality in the world and around us was contemplated with a view to finding our own position in that world. And that's a place where certain tasks were carried out with this regard. In other words, it was a military scientific institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand now what you mean, or I better understand now what you mean. You indicated that the strategic research that was done was responding to the military and political reality in the world, and you contemplated a view to finding our own position in that world. When you are talking about our own position, whose position are you referring to, sir? What army are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Obviously I'm talking about military and political relations and when it comes to the military, that part concerned our own jobs, our own profession, and political, obviously implies that everything we do in the world has political significance. I'm now sharing with you my own thoughts because I found it very difficult as a human being and as a soldier to think along the lines of my superior, whoever that may have been. I always thought it from the position that I had joined the Yugoslav People's Army voluntarily, that that was my own military, that I was a citizen of a state that I loved, and that when it came to relations in the world, primarily military and political relations in the world, and the position of my own state and my own military, I always had to uphold my own opinion, an opinion that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that you have a fair number of opinions and I promise you during the course of our discussion we will be exploring those opinions. What I'd like to do now just for the moment is understand how long were you at this particular institute? And by that, how many years or months were you there before you moved to your next position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I started working at the centre for strategic research and studies, i.e., in the institute for strategic research within the centre sometime in September 1984. In the meantime, from November 1986 until August, July or August, I'm not quite sure, 1988, I was a member of the delegation, as I already started to explain, of the SFRY, that attended the conference on the European co-operation and security, which was held in Vienna. I would like to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: -- that this conference on the European security and co-operation, later was renamed organisation of the security and co-operation in Europe. As a member of the delegation in Vienna, I received a message from Belgrade to return to my country because pursuant to an order of my superior officer, I was transferred to the officer of Veljko Kadijevic, colonel-general, who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Who was the secretary for national defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you went in 1988 as a member of the delegation involved in the conference on the European co-operation and security in Vienna, what was your purpose, and by that I mean why did you go to that particular conference? What were your responsibilities and duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. Guy-Smith, I'd like to say that I became a member of the delegation in, I think, November of 1986. Not in 1988 as you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me in that regard. With regard to your duties and obligations, what were those, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The centre of the armed forces for strategic research and studies was considered to be a scientific institution and that it would be best placed to follow and monitor new developments in Europe and in the world. The meetings on the European security and operation had a different set of the topics, one of them was building measures, confidence building measures for co-operation. As a member of this institute, I was appointed a member of this delegation, and I believe that my superior had noticed that I had certain knowledge in that particular field, which I had not acquired in a regular manner because nobody asked me about that, but I rather believe that what was going on and what was happening at this conference on co-operation and security in Europe was something that the majority of people around me were not able to comprehend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I understand what your view is of what was occurring. My question to you is, what were your duties with regard to this specific conference?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I had the status of a member of the delegation and that of a military advisor as well. That was the customary procedure applied by all member states of the conference. Only some major countries had more members that constituted a whole military team. For example, such big countries like the USA, Russia, France, and Germany had their military teams that were at the disposal of the head of their respective delegations. So my role was to advise the head of the delegation and to act as a military representative whenever it was necessary and customary. When I say customary, I don't think that it was something strictly prescribed, but it meant that there shouldn't be any significant deviations from the practices pursued by other countries and states.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this specific conference before you were ordered, as you mentioned a bit earlier, to return to Belgrade, did you make contacts with representatives from other foreign delegations such as the ones you've mentioned just a moment ago, United States, Russia, France, and Germany? And all I'm asking you is whether you made contact with them, nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had regular contacts during the sessions and we had similar contacts on various Working Groups. However, the most important talks at the time, at least in my mind, were the talks held within the group that were called at the time neutral and non-aligned countries. We represented a group of countries. And another group were NATO members and the third group were members of the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. As you sit here today, can you tell us who were the members of the -- who were the NATO members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The NATO members were, of course, members of NATO. There were 16 of them at the time, and NATO stands for North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you part of that group? Were you part of the NATO members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which part were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in the group of neutral and non-aligned countries. Our partners in that group, just for the sake of illustration, were, for example, Sweden, Finland -- I think my mike is off. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Okay. So Sweden, Finland, Switzerland, Austria, Malta, Cyprus, the whole east sea, San Marino, Lichtenstein, and I apologise if I've forgot some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned a third group, you also mentioned a third group, those were the Warsaw Pact members. As you sit here today, can you recall who was involved at that time representing the Warsaw Pact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The Warsaw Pact was represented and led, first of all, by the USSR, and it included Poland, Czechoslovakia, the Democratic Republic of Germany, the so-called east Germany, Romania, Bulgaria, and I think that's about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that, if I understood your evidence thus far correctly, but at some point in time while you were at the conference or close to that point in time you were ordered to return to Belgrade and to become part of a group with Mr. Kadijevic, is that correct? And I do apologise for the leading, question, Mr. Thomas, I understand that it is one.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, your question is not a leading one. I already said that I reported to this body, which was called the office of the federal secretary for national defence. I think that was in May or June 1998, and at that time Colonel-General Kadijevic was the secretary and his predecessor was Branko Mamula.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me make sure that we're correct on the dates. The translation indicates it was May or June of 1998. Is that an accurate date, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know exactly when this replacement was carried out, and I'm talking about the secretary for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My concern is the date of 1998 and whether that's an accurate reflection of the time that you were called back to work with Lieutenant-Colonel Kadijevic or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm probably thinking about all these years when these things were happening with Yugoslavia. But this was in 1988, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated that you were called back to the office for the federal secretary for national defence. Now, was that a civilian office, a military office, under whose jurisdiction was that office, if you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: It was a military institution directly subordinated to the federal secretary for national defence. At the time serving in this office were only professional servicemen, commissioned and non-commissioned officers. Civilian posts were filled by a number of individuals doing the so-called technical or administrative jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were called back to work with Lieutenant-Colonel Kadijevic what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: He was colonel-general, that's what Mr. Kadijevic was at the time, colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And what were your duties when you were called back to work with Colonel-General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I became an advisor for liaisons with the west. That meant with the western countries, and for the sake of clarity, let me tell you that those were the countries popularly called at the time capitalist countries whereas today they would be dubbed as western democracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you've used that particular term, they were called capitalist countries, was the country that you harkened from a capitalist county or was it some other form of politicals or economic reality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The primary designation that is contained in the name of my country, which was called Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, meant that this country had a single party system and a socialist system including in the sphere of economy, that is to say the system was organised in a socialist way which governed all the relations including economic ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say it governed all the relations including the economic ones, did that include the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, including the military. In the then Yugoslavia, these relations and the structure in the military were organised in the way that was employed in the so-called socialist country to the extent that the then Yugoslavia did not differ from the so-called classic socialist countries. In other words, that meant the countries that were members of the Warsaw Pact. However, there were differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need to explore those differences at this time, but were there differences to your knowledge, based upon the experience that you had had by that time with western or capitalist countries as it related to the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, there were differences, and I'm going to give you perhaps the most important one. The weapon stockpiles held by the Yugoslav People's Army consisted of the equipment and weapon procured from the Soviet Union, the very fact that we had weapons and military equipment either received or bought from the western countries speaks for itself. What I mean by this is that we had never been a classic socialist country. If we had been one, then we would have been a member of the Warsaw Pact. That opportunity came up in 1948, but fortunately, that did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've just mentioned something in your last answer which I'd like to explore with you for a minute, which is, you said "the very fact that we had weapons and military equipment, either received or bought from the western countries speaks for itself." First of all, I'd like to see if we have some understanding here with regard to what you mean by military equipment that was purchased from western countries. Could you identify for us at that point in time what western countries you were involved in military purchases for weapons with? And by that point in time, I'm referring to 1988?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, there were weapons and equipment that originated from the west. Maybe this is an imprecise term but it is well known and we received these stockpiles after the Second World War. These stockpiles included tanks, armoured vehicles, personnel carriers, and other things. However, after 1948 when the relations with the Soviet Union became sour and when Yugoslavia became isolated from those quarters and was exposed to pressure, it was very seriously attempted to attract Yugoslavia to the west and for it to become a member of the NATO. That did not happen. However, we concluded a treaty with Greece and Turkey who were NATO members which meant that in the event of an aggression from the east, these countries would be co-operating with us. In that sense, the US gave us, or rather, delivered at favourable prices modern equipment and military materiel. That happened in the period between 1952 and 1956. If it is of any significance, I might say that they gave us Sherman and patent tanks and even some supersonic aircraft. So by using one of those aircraft, General Lekic was the first to break the sound barrier over Yugoslavia. He flew from the airfield in Batajnica, and we were very proud of that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, if I may just ask, I'm not quite sure where we are going with all this. We've been at this topic for quite a long time. I'm not sure where you are going with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so far --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I mean, I didn't expect to be back in 1956, I'm interested -- I find it to be interesting to note when someone broke the sound barrier, however, I think--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certain things are very interesting historically, but you've got a job to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think you and I are in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to move you forward to 1900 -- and we were in 1988 and I'd like to go to your next responsibility.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: From my position in the office of the federal secretary for national defence, in March of 1992, I was transferred because of the need of the service to the operations group for liaisons with international forces and missions. I remained in this post and I was first a deputy and later on I became assistant chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I had like to stop you there for a moment. You said that you were transferred to that position in March of 1992. What were your duties at that time in March of 1992 with regard to liaisons with international forces and missions? First of all, if you could identify what international forces, that would be of some help.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I carried out these duties in the office of the federal secretary but the scope of this work suddenly increased as the crisis became more acute, and the participation of the international community --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Vuksic, once again my question is, could you identify for us the specific international forces that you were dealing with at that time? When you say international forces, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to international representatives, international missions, and international forces. International representatives were representatives of all international organisations that were involved in the Yugoslav crises. At the time, it was the European community, the United Nations, and NATO indirectly. First there was a monitoring mission of the European community which arrived after the conflict in Slovenia in the then Yugoslavia. Also OSCE played a significant role as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. When you indicated there was a monitoring mission of the European community which arrived after the conflict in Slovenia, could you kindly give us an approximate date as to when that particular monitoring mission arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember a specific date because I don't know which would be day one, however, already towards the end of July the conflict, which was over in the meantime, produced certain consequences and eventually the withdrawal of the JNA and all these processes were monitored by the EC monitoring mission. So we can say that it happened in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Stop you there then. Let me stop you there then, please. You indicated that the conflict which was over in the meantime produced certain consequences and eventually the withdrawal of the JNA. My question to you is, from what geographic regions did the JNA withdraw from? And I'm asking you very specifically what regions did they withdraw from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: At the time it withdrew from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the JNA withdrew from Slovenia, did it withdraw from any other areas in the, what I will now call for the moment the -- what I'll now call for the moment the former SFRY? Were there any specific regions that it withdrew from or republics or states or geographic areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Following the clashes in the second half of 1991 and thanks to the mediation of the CMM, the JNA withdrew from the remaining garrisons across Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from withdrawing from the remaining garrisons across Croatia, did the JNA withdraw from any other regions, areas, republics, states, or geographic locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: At the time back in 1991, the JNA still had a presence in the other republics, meaning Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Macedonia. It is understood that it also had a presence in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the JNA's presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina changed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Following quite dramatic developments, the JNA was to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 19th of May, 1992. Nevertheless, there were several garrisons in Bosnia-Herzegovina that had been blocked by armed units organised by Muslims and Croats to be as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were these several garrisons successful in withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina after they had been -- as I understand it, after they had been blocked by the unit that is you've mentioned organised by the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Not a single withdrawal went smoothly without causing trouble and headaches. It was all on the verge of armed conflict all the time. Suffice it for us now to mention two. The withdrawal from Tuzla and the withdrawal of the command of the 2nd Army Military District from Sarajevo. When tragic developments occurred because the JNA was attacked in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the withdrawal of Tuzla, do you recall the date of that withdrawal in terms of the way that you've put it, the tragic developments that occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber if you know what occurred at the time the JNA was withdrawing from Tuzla and it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The JNA convoy was in the process of withdrawing and was on its way through the city of Tuzla. This was a route that had been pre-agreed. They were following all the steps that had been agreed, and all of a sudden --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You say this has been pre-agreed. By whom was it pre-agreed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: It was agreed by, as far as I know, representatives of the local authorities, meaning the mayor of Tuzla, in the simplest of terms, and at least the garrison commander, a general at the time, but the agreement could not have been concluded without the presence of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "ECMM," could you please identify those letters for us so we know what they mean, so we are using the actual name as opposed to an acronym?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The monitoring mission, you mean. The European Community Monitoring Mission. That was the official name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the JNA convoy was in the process of withdrawing and was on its way through the city of Tuzla, this was the route that had been pre-agreed. What occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: As I said, the convoy came under attack. One of those responsible stood trial before a Belgrade court. I can't say how many casualties there were, those wounded and killed, because as a rule I do my best to forget information like that as quickly as I can regardless of the origin of the victims. I don't consider that to be particularly important, nor is it something that I wish to memorise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. You indicated there was another incident that was a withdrawal by the JNA from Sarajevo. Do you recall when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: It occurred on Dobrovoljacka Street. An agreement had been reached with UNPROFOR who were already present in the area. The Sarajevo UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I need to interrupt you there. This is the first time that you've mentioned UNPROFOR. Could you please tell us who you are referring to when you say "UNPROFOR?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I failed to complete my previous answer. When I said that I was working with certain delegates and representatives of certain missions and forces, when I said mission, I said the ECMM, represented by individuals who came on behalf of certain organisations. When I said forces, I meant the United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, the protection force of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So you indicated an agreement had been reached with UNPROFOR who were already present in the area, the Sarajevo UNPROFOR command. And who was that agreement, if you know, reached between; the UNPROFOR and what other institution, organisation, state, or political or military body?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Between the Muslim side on the one hand, the JNA on the other, and on behalf of UNPROFOR, the whole process was monitored and the withdrawal was brokered by the then Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR, General MacKenzie, a Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I know I interrupted you to get some more specific information, but I had asked you earlier what happened on the 6th of May, 1992 on Dobrovoljacka Street, if you could tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This event is also something that is being considered and reviewed by the Belgrade court. Commissioned officers and NCOs numbering among their ranks no more than a few privates from the military district command in Sarajevo suddenly came under attack, from all sides. Those men were quite literally massacred. Although as I said I'm not fond of remembering figures of that kind, I believe a total of 46 men were killed. One of those who were seriously wounded was a Muslim general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to recall the name. Nevertheless, I knew the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say he was a Muslim general, he was a Muslim general in what army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: He was still a member of the JNA. He was serving with the command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo. He was a Muslim and this fact at the very least shows that the JNA at the time were still a multiethnic army. It also shows that there may have been the occasional Serb on the other side, such as the former colonel Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After this incident on the 6th of May, 1992, were the remaining officers and soldiers who were still alive, able to withdraw from the area as had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The wounded and killed had to be taken care of in Sarajevo itself. As for the remainder of the convoy, it had by this time already crossed the bridge that at the time divided the two warring sides, the Muslim and the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic had already been released. He was the Muslim leader at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: This was a condition for the convoy of the 2nd Military District Command to be allowed to peacefully pass through. Once the convoy had crossed the bridge which at the time served as an informal confrontation line, and once Alija Izetbegovic had been released, which means that under the circumstances, the Serbian side was complying with everything that had been agreed, and in the plain view of General MacKenzie, the convoy came under attack. The remainder travelled on in a more or less organised manner until they could cross to Serb-held territory, territory that at the time was under the control of the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: At that point in time what was your function? Were you still involved in the job as a liaison with the international organisations and institutions that you've previously mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: If you look at what I've said already, you can tell that I was the deputy head of the operative group for liaising with international missions and organisations. Not a liaison officer. And yes, I was informed about that, about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the incident that you've just mentioned, did you have any conversations and/or contact with members of UNPROFOR or any other international organisations concerning those two incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: I must say this occurred quite unexpectedly and in such a dreadful way. As a result, we were all appalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is once again -- excuse me, sir. My question is really quite specific. Did you have any conversations and/or contact with members of UNPROFOR or any other international organisations concerning those two incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What contact did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Those were regular contacts, but those never occurred just for their own sake. Those weren't meetings that were strictly about making contact. There are reasons for that. My rank within the hierarchy was too low at the time for me to be the person shedding light on incidents such as this one. The discontent that I voiced during my conversations with these representatives was a mere addition to things that were happening at a higher level. Speaking of the Sarajevo incident, General MacKenzie himself was unable to explain at the time how something like that could possibly have come about. Later on, in his book of memoirs, I don't remember reading anything he wrote about that. I do however, know that he was extremely critical when he wrote about the side that carried out the attack on the JNA convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. After these incidents occurred and you had, as you told us, voiced your discontent in conversations that you had with representatives, did you continue in your position within the JNA as a liaison -- I'm sorry, in your position with the JNA involving -- being involved in liaising with the international organisations that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remained in that position. The operative group continued to do its job under circumstances that were very difficult and now changed. The UNPROFOR command because of all the attacks had to move from Sarajevo to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a question for you here, which is, when the JNA -- after the JNA withdrew from Sarajevo, did you remain as an officer in the JNA, did you become part of another army, was there a change or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: No. There was no change. I remained in my position as chief of the operative group, and I was still a member of the JNA. No longer in a formal sense though, because on the 27th of April, it had changed its name and was now called the Army of the FRY. From the 27th on, I was a member of the VJ, which was now it's official name until the FRY ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a question for you and I'm hoping you can help us. You indicated that you were part of, I believe, the army which was at that point called the SSNO. There was one entire army. And I'm going back now to 1988. Now, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a badly framed question. I'll redo the whole thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the whole question of SSNO, where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It comes from my head. It's in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you became a member of the VJ, as opposed to when you were part of the JNA, was the military structure of the VJ and the JNA in terms of the entirety of defence, military defence, the same? If you understand my question, which once again may be badly phrased.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Guy-Smith, small correction. The SSNO is not an army. It's the Federal Secretariat for the National Defence. The army at the time was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that the SSNO is not an army, it's a Federal Secretariat for the National Defence, what institutional organs comprised the Federal Secretariat for the National Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat for the National Defence at the time comprised the General Staff of the JNA; the deputy federal secretary for national defence; the assistance for the rear, which is not the same as logistics; the assistance for political and legal affairs; the assistance for the military colony, and a number of subordinate organisations. This was an administrative and command component, military component, within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The federal secretary for national defence was at the same time the most senior soldier as well as the superior of the Chief of the General Staff. He was also the Commander-in-Chief of the army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Commander-in-Chief of the army? Was the Commander-in-Chief not the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was superior to all the members of the JNA in a disciplinary sense, in a command sense, and in a administrative sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my question, sir. I'm not talking about members of the JNA. I'm talking about the president of the country. Was this Commander-in-Chief of the army not the president of the country, that's my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, I'll add one thing to that, which is the date that we are referring to, because there is a -- there are shifts that occur within the structure here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say that there was -- are you saying that there was a time when there was no president in the -- in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying that, but I think it's important that we deal with dates here. That's the only issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could answer His Honour's question, we'd be appreciative.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, while answering some of the previous questions, perhaps I should have added that our army was organised in the same way as other armies of the socialist or communist block where the federal secretary was a military professional superior to any members of the army in terms of command, in terms of discipline, in terms of administration. I know what you have in mind, the Commander-in-Chief was Tito while he was alive. Following Tito's death, it was the Presidency of the FRY, or rather, the SFRY as a collective body that was the Commander-in-Chief. This was a collective body which remained Commander-in-Chief until the break-up of Yugoslavia. When the FRY was established, the Supreme Defence Council was established too, comprising the president of the FRY and the presidents of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro. The federal secretary of national defence, who is now minister, was no longer a military professional, but rather a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the last part of your answer, which is the federal secretary of national defence who is now a minister was no longer a military professional, but rather a civilian, he was a minister or she, but he was a minister of what, what was his title? Minister of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC
utterances.text: The first minister of defence, I think, was the late Pavle Bulatovic. He was a defence minister and a member of the cabinet in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Sorry, Mr. Vuksic, we have not been able to finish with you unfortunately, so you'll have to come back tomorrow again at 2.00 in the afternoon in the same courtroom. In the meantime, now that you've taken the witness-stand to testify, you may no longer discuss this case with anybody until you are excused from testifying, especially not the lawyers for Mr. Perisic. Okay. Then we stand adjourned to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be back here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for understanding. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
